items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person in the world from birth until death”.
options: United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child
items.answer: Human rights
items.markingKey: Human rights: basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person in the world from birth until death. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the weight of the air pressing down on the Earth’s surface, measured in millibars (hPa)”.
items.answer: Air pressure
items.markingKey: Air pressure: the weight of the air pressing down on the Earth’s surface, measured in millibars (hPa). [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “A sustainable city only needs to focus on the environment.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Sustainability also includes social (housing, services, safety) and economic (jobs) needs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Estimated deaths in the Second World War (millions, military then civilian): Japan 2.1 and 0.6; Poland 0.2 and 5.6; Germany 5.3 and 1.5; United Kingdom 0.38 and 0.07; Soviet Union 8.7 and 17. Estimates vary between historians. Which of these countries had the greatest total number of deaths?
items.answer: Soviet Union
items.markingKey: Soviet Union: 25.7 million. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the number of deaths from an earthquake does not depend only on its magnitude.
items.answer: It also depends on depth, distance from cities, population density, building quality, time of day, preparedness and the speed of rescue; e.g. Haiti 2010 (magnitude 7.0) killed far more than Chile 2010 (8.8).
items.markingKey: 1 mark factors; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: Study Source A, a report on the Congo by the British consul Roger Casement, 1904 (adapted). “In village after village the people told me that soldiers were sent to punish them if the rubber brought in was too little. Many had been killed or had their hands cut off, and whole districts were deserted.” Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of the treatment of people in the Congo Free State that Source A does not show.
items.answer: The number of people who died overall or the profits Leopold made from rubber.
items.markingKey: 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the fencing off of open fields and common land into separate, privately owned farms”.
items.answer: Enclosure
items.markingKey: Enclosure: the fencing off of open fields and common land into separate, privately owned farms. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the total value of goods and services produced by a country in a year divided by its population”.
items.answer: GDP per capita
items.markingKey: GDP per capita: the total value of goods and services produced by a country in a year divided by its population. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A 1:25 000 map shows more detail than a 1:50 000 map.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It is a larger scale: 1 cm represents 250 m instead of 500 m, so features are shown bigger and in more detail.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A survey of 100 residents in a diverse neighbourhood asked “Do you feel you belong to this community?” Results: “Strongly” 36, “A little” 22, “Not at all” 42. What percentage felt they belonged at least a little?
A student writes: “All deserts are hot all year round.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many deserts have cold winters or cold nights, and some (e.g. Antarctica or the Gobi) are cold deserts; deserts are defined by low precipitation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Most migrants move from poorer countries to Europe and North America.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many migrants move within their own region, e.g. from South Asia to the Gulf, or within Africa; most refugees are hosted by neighbouring countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Read Source A carefully. “The cartoon shows Germany as a figure lying on a guillotine while Wilson, Clemenceau and Lloyd George stand over it. The caption reads: “The verdict of Versailles.”” (A German cartoon published in 1919, described in words.) What can you infer from Source A about German reactions to the Treaty of Versailles?
items.answer: Germans saw the treaty as a cruel punishment, almost a death sentence, imposed by the Allied leaders.
items.markingKey: 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the Tōhoku earthquake (magnitude 9.0) had a much higher economic cost than the Nepal earthquake (magnitude 7.8). (b) Explain why the earthquake in Haiti (2010) killed so many more people than the stronger earthquake in Chile (2010).
items.answer: (a) Japan is a high-income country with expensive buildings, infrastructure, ports, factories and a nuclear power plant in the affected area; the tsunami destroyed property worth far more, so costs (estimated at over US$200 billion) were much higher. (b) Haiti is a low-income country: buildings in Port-au-Prince were poorly constructed and densely packed, building codes were not enforced, and emergency services were weak; Chile had strict building codes and experienced earthquake planning. Haiti’s epicentre was also very close to the capital and shallow.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark value of property/infrastructure; 1 mark tsunami/nuclear damage [2] (b) 1 mark buildings/codes; 1 mark emergency capacity; 1 mark location/depth [3]

items.stem: The table shows the approximate number of independent states in Africa: 1950: 4, 1956: 8, 1960: 27, 1965: 37, 1975: 48, 1990: 52. (a) Calculate the increase in independent states between 1960 and 1965. (b) Explain why some countries became independent much later, in the 1970s and after.
items.answer: (a) 10 (b) Colonial powers with many settlers or a dictatorship (Portugal until 1974, white-minority rule in Rhodesia and South Africa’s control of Namibia) resisted; independence came after long wars.
items.markingKey: (a) 37 − 27 [1] (b) 1 mark reason; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: A student investigating the impact of railways in the 1830s and 1840s finds Source A. Source A: a newspaper report on the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, September 1830 (adapted). “The engines drew carriages filled with passengers at a speed of more than twenty miles an hour. The whole route was lined with crowds who had come to see this wonder of the age.” Suggest the purpose of Source A. Explain your answer.
items.answer: To report a major public event and interest readers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Globalisation only affects trade in goods.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It also involves services, money, migration, ideas, culture, information and environmental issues.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A class in Mumbai is investigating whether people feel safe walking in different parts of their neighbourhood. Identify one source of secondary data that would help, and explain why.
items.answer: Crime statistics published by the local police, because it gives evidence from a longer time period or a wider area than the students can collect.
items.markingKey: 1 mark source; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of the first-past-the-post electoral system.
items.answer: Advantage: simple, quick to count, usually produces strong single-party governments and a clear local representative. Disadvantage: seats do not match vote share, smaller parties win few seats and many votes are “wasted”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Annual average carbon dioxide concentration measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (parts per million): 1960: 317, 1970: 326, 1980: 339, 1990: 354, 2000: 370, 2010: 390, 2020: 414. (a) Calculate the percentage increase compared with the pre-industrial level of about 280 ppm, using the 2020 value. (b) Explain the main reasons for the increase.
items.answer: (a) 48% (b) Burning fossil fuels for power, industry and transport, and deforestation, especially as industrial economies such as China and India grew.
items.markingKey: (a) (414 − 280) ÷ 280 × 100 [2] (b) 1 mark fossil fuels; 1 mark deforestation/growth [2]

items.stem: The table shows population and area for three regions of a country. River Delta: population 30 000 000  area 25 000 km². Coastal Plain: population 480 000  area 1 200 km². Capital Region: population 60 000 000  area 12 000 km². Suggest two reasons why Coastal Plain is sparsely populated.
items.answer: Farming land with few large towns, or flood risk.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “War memorials only remember soldiers from Britain and France.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Memorials such as India Gate and the Menin Gate name soldiers from across the British Empire, and countries around the world have their own memorials.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Kwame argues that prediction is the most effective way of reducing the impact of tectonic hazards. To what extent do you agree? Give reasons for and against before reaching a judgement.
items.answer: Agree: Monitoring allowed the Pinatubo evacuation (1991); tsunami warnings give time to reach high ground. Disagree: Earthquakes cannot be predicted precisely, so protection (building design) saves more lives. Planning – hazard maps, drills, land-use rules – reduces vulnerability. Warnings only help if people receive them and know what to do. Judgement: Prediction is vital for volcanoes and tsunamis, but protection and planning matter more for earthquakes.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Source D is taken from Jawaharlal Nehru’s speech to India’s Constituent Assembly, 14-15 August 1947. It says: “At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) Is Source D a primary or a secondary source? Give a reason for your answer. (b) What can you infer from Source D about how Indian leaders presented independence? (c) Suggest the purpose of Source D. Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Primary source: it comes from the time being studied, or from someone directly involved in the events. (b) Independence was presented as a historic, almost miraculous new beginning for India. (c) To celebrate independence and inspire Indians with hope and unity at a difficult moment.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct type; 1 mark reason based on its origin/date [2] (b) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (c) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: A student investigating the aims and failure of Chartism finds Source A. Source A: the People’s Charter, 1838 (adapted summary of its six points). “A vote for every man twenty-one years of age; the secret ballot; no property qualification for Members of Parliament; payment of Members; equal electoral districts; annual parliaments.” (a) Suggest the purpose of Source A. Explain your answer. (b) Explain one reason why Source A may be reliable and one reason why it may not be reliable. (c) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of what the Chartists wanted that Source A does not show.
items.answer: (a) To set out the movement’s demands clearly so that people would sign the petitions to Parliament. (b) May be reliable: it is the official statement of the Chartists’ aims, written at the time. May not be reliable: it shows aims, not how much support there was or what methods Chartists used. (c) That women were not included, or that the petitions of 1839, 1842 and 1848 were rejected.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2] (b) 2 marks for each explained reason based on provenance (author, date, purpose) [4] (c) 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that governments, not individuals, should take the lead in achieving the SDGs.
items.answer: Agree: Governments control laws, budgets and international agreements, and can act at large scale. Disagree: Businesses, NGOs, communities and individuals also make a difference, e.g. reducing waste, campaigning, volunteering. Many local projects are led by communities. Individual pressure pushes governments to act. Judgement: Governments must lead, but the goals need action at every level.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: In a survey, 180 people were asked about how safe they feel in the park. Results: very safe 30, safe 32, unsafe 23, very unsafe 95. (a) Calculate the angle of the sector for “unsafe” on a pie chart. (b) Suggest one other way to present the data and explain an advantage.
items.answer: (a) 46° (b) A bar chart: makes it easier to compare the exact size of each category.
items.markingKey: (a) 23/180 × 360° = 46° [2] (b) 1 mark method; 1 mark advantage [2]

items.stem: How far do you agree that peaceful protest is the most effective way for citizens to bring about change? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
items.answer: Agree: Peaceful campaigns win public sympathy and media attention: the Montgomery bus boycott, Gandhi’s Salt March, Fridays for Future. Disagree: Voting and elections change governments and laws directly. Lobbying, petitions and legal challenges can achieve change quietly. Some groups (e.g. some suffragettes) argued militant action was needed when peaceful methods were ignored. Judgement: Peaceful protest is powerful, especially combined with voting, lobbying and legal action.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Two places lie at about 52° N. Place P is on the west coast, facing prevailing westerly winds from the ocean: July average 19 °C, January 6 °C. Place Q is 1500 km inland: July average 23 °C, January -2 °C. (a) Explain why Q has a larger range than P. (b) Name the type of climate P and Q are likely to have.
items.answer: (a) Q is far from the sea: land heats quickly in summer and cools quickly in winter (continentality); P is moderated by the sea, which heats and cools slowly, and by mild westerly winds from the ocean. (b) P: temperate maritime; Q: continental.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark land heats/cools quickly; 1 mark sea moderates P; 1 mark winds [3] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “The growth of megacities brings more benefits than problems.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: jobs and wealth; inequality; housing.
items.answer: Agree: Megacities concentrate jobs, investment, universities and services and produce a large share of national wealth (e.g. Mumbai). Disagree: Rapid growth leads to informal settlements, congestion, pollution and pressure on water and sanitation (e.g. Lagos, Dhaka). Inequality between rich and poor is often extreme. Judgement: Megacities offer major opportunities, but benefits outweigh problems only where growth is well planned and managed.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.answer: Colony

items.stem: A revision website states: “The hole in the ozone layer is the main cause of global warming.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Ozone depletion and global warming are different problems; warming is caused mainly by greenhouse gases such as CO₂.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.answer: Primary source: it comes from the time being studied, or from someone directly involved in the events.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by interdependence, using an example.
items.answer: Countries rely on each other: e.g. Europe imports smartphones made in China while China imports European machinery; a problem in one place (such as the Suez blockage) affects others.
items.markingKey: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: Results in five constituencies (votes for Green Party, Workers’ Party, People’s Party): C1: 6611, 7220, 7776; C2: 7963, 4276, 6228; C3: 5505, 3991, 6826; C4: 8573, 5623, 2350; C5: 5368, 7209, 6044. The election uses first-past-the-post. Suggest two reasons why turnout in elections may be low.
items.answer: Voters feel their vote will not change the result (safe seats); distrust of politicians; difficulty getting to polling stations; lack of interest or information.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.answer: Informal settlement
items.markingKey: Informal settlement: an area of unplanned housing built by residents on land they do not legally own, usually lacking basic services (a slum or shanty town). [1]

items.answer: Cholera

items.stem: A student writes: “A hypothesis must be proved correct for an investigation to be successful.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Finding that the evidence does not support a hypothesis is still a valid result; the conclusion explains why.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.answer: Primary source: it comes from the time being studied, or from someone directly involved in the events.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct type; 1 mark reason based on its origin/date [2]

items.stem: Explain how hazard mapping can reduce risk.
items.answer: It shows which areas are most dangerous (e.g. lahar paths, liquefaction zones), so governments can stop building there, plan evacuation routes and place emergency services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies danger zones; 1 mark use in planning [2]

items.stem: Explain how relief rainfall forms and why it leads to a rain shadow.
items.answer: Moist air is forced to rise over mountains, cools, condenses and forms clouds and rain on the windward side; descending air on the leeward side warms and is dry, creating a rain shadow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark rising/cooling; 1 mark condensation/rain; 1 mark leeward dry [3]

items.stem: Estimated deaths in the Second World War (millions, military then civilian): United Kingdom 0.38 and 0.07; USA 0.41 and 0.01; Soviet Union 8.7 and 17; Germany 5.3 and 1.5; China 3.8 and 16. Estimates vary between historians. Explain why estimates of deaths in the Second World War vary.
items.answer: Records were destroyed or never kept, especially in occupied areas; borders changed; deaths from famine and disease are hard to count; governments sometimes changed figures for political reasons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “A higher infant mortality rate usually indicates a lower level of development.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It reflects poor health care, nutrition, clean water and sanitation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A group of students in Auckland is campaigning for a community vegetable garden on unused land. In two weeks their petition has collected 400 signatures in a community of about 3 000 people. (a) Calculate the percentage of the community who have signed. (b) Identify who the students should try to persuade, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 13.3% (b) The local council or school leadership (decision-makers), because they have the power and budget to make the change; also local media to raise awareness.
items.markingKey: (a) 400 ÷ 3000 × 100 [1] (b) 1 mark target; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: The table shows population and area for three regions of a country. Northern District: population 72 000  area 800 km². Highland Region: population 32 000  area 800 km². Capital Region: population 21 000 000  area 6 000 km². Calculate the population density of Northern District.
items.answer: 90 people per km²

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Britain had to import most of the coal used in its factories.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Britain had large coalfields of its own, in places such as South Wales, the North East and the Midlands.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why the Indian Rebellion of 1857 led to changes in how India was governed.
items.answer: The British government ended East India Company rule and took direct control (1858), creating the British Raj; it also reorganised the army and became more cautious about interfering with religion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark Crown takes over; 1 mark further change [2]

items.answer: (a) about 1 024 times (b) A seismometer (seismograph).

items.stem: A student writes: “Soldiers spent all their time in the front-line trench fighting.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Soldiers rotated between front-line, support and reserve trenches and rest areas; much time was spent on routine work and waiting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: How far do you agree that the Sustainable Development Goals are too ambitious to be achieved by 2030? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: funding; value of targets; COVID-19 and conflict.
items.answer: Agree: UN reports show many targets are off track; COVID-19, conflict and climate change have reversed progress on poverty and hunger. Disagree: Goals set direction and focus funding; some targets (e.g. electricity access, child mortality) have improved significantly. Ambitious goals inspire action by governments, businesses and citizens. Judgement: Many goals will probably not be fully met by 2030, but they remain valuable as a shared plan for action.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A survey of 80 residents in a diverse neighbourhood asked “Do you feel you belong to this community?” Results: “Strongly” 39, “A little” 19, “Not at all” 22. (a) Suggest two reasons why some residents may not feel they belong. (b) Suggest two actions the local council could take to increase belonging. (c) Explain one limitation of this survey.
items.answer: (a) They may have recently arrived, face language barriers or discrimination, have few local friends or family, or feel excluded from local decisions. (b) Community festivals and events; language classes; youth clubs and sports; involving residents in decisions; tackling discrimination. (c) A small sample may not represent the whole neighbourhood; people may not answer honestly; “belonging” means different things to different people; who was asked and where may bias results.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) 1 mark limitation; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: Nadia argues that the Demographic Transition Model is a useful way to understand population change in all countries. To what extent do you agree? Give reasons for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: disease; European experience.
items.answer: Agree: It describes the experience of many countries, such as the UK, well. It helps predict future changes in birth and death rates. Disagree: It was based on European experience; some countries moved through stages much faster or got “stuck”. It ignores migration and government policies (e.g. China’s one-child policy). Diseases such as HIV/AIDS raised death rates in some countries. Judgement: It is a useful general model but needs adapting for individual countries.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: How far do you agree that workers’ own protests did more than the government to improve working conditions? Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
items.answer: Agree: Trade unions and strikes won better pay; protests over Tolpuddle won a pardon; Chartist pressure kept reform in the public eye. Disagree: Laws passed by Parliament (Factory Acts, Mines Act, Public Health Acts) changed conditions for millions. Middle-class reformers such as Shaftesbury, Chadwick and Oastler drove much change. Protest was often repressed, e.g. Peterloo 1819. Judgement: Government action had the widest effect, but it often came in response to pressure from workers and reformers.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student investigating how British rule affected India finds Source D. Source D: a historian writing in 2005 about the British Empire in India. “British rule brought railways, telegraphs and universities to India, but they were built mainly to serve British trade and administration, and Indian industries such as hand-weaving declined.” (a) What can you infer from Source D about the effects of British rule in India? (b) Suggest the purpose of Source D. Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) The effects of British rule were mixed: there was new infrastructure, but it mainly benefited Britain and harmed some Indian industries. (b) To give a balanced interpretation of British rule based on research.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (b) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: “Decolonisation happened mainly because European powers were weakened by the Second World War.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: colonial wars; economic weakness; superpowers and the UN.
items.answer: Agree: Britain and France were economically exhausted and dependent on US loans. Japan’s wartime victories ended the myth of European invincibility. Disagree: Nationalist movements and leaders (Gandhi, Nkrumah, Kenyatta) made colonies ungovernable or won elections. The USA, USSR and the UN supported self-determination. Wars such as Algeria and Indochina were costly and unpopular. Judgement: The war created the conditions, but nationalist pressure decided when and how colonies became independent.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Scientists measure that the Pacific plate sliding past the North American plate along the San Andreas Fault move past each other at about 4 cm per year. (a) Calculate how far they move in 100 000 years  in kilometres. (b) Name the type of plate boundary. (c) Explain what causes the plates to move.
items.answer: (a) 4 km (b) Conservative (c) Convection currents in the mantle, together with ridge push and slab pull.

items.stem: “A school weather station can give data that is just as reliable as an official weather station.” Discuss this view, explaining points for and against, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: siting; consistency of readings; equipment.
items.answer: Agree: Simple instruments (rain gauge, max-min thermometer, anemometer) can be accurate if sited and read correctly. Disagree: School sites are often sheltered by buildings, affecting wind and rain readings. Readings may be missed at weekends and holidays or taken at different times. Official stations use calibrated, automatic equipment and strict siting rules. Judgement: School data can be useful and fairly reliable, but rarely as reliable as official stations without careful siting and routine.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a system of government in which citizens choose their leaders in free and fair elections”.
items.answer: Democracy
items.markingKey: Democracy: a system of government in which citizens choose their leaders in free and fair elections. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a reason that makes people want to leave a place, such as unemployment, conflict or drought”.
items.answer: Push factor
items.markingKey: Push factor: a reason that makes people want to leave a place, such as unemployment, conflict or drought. [1]

items.stem: Explain why inventions in spinning led to inventions in weaving.
items.answer: Faster spinning machines (jenny, water frame, mule) produced more thread than hand-loom weavers could use, creating demand for a faster weaving machine – the power loom.
items.markingKey: 1 mark imbalance; 1 mark leads to power loom [2]

items.stem: A group in Riyadh is investigating how a local memorial is used to remember people who died in war. Write a suitable hypothesis for this investigation.
items.answer: The memorial is mainly visited on Remembrance Day.
items.markingKey: 1 mark testable statement linked to the enquiry [1]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of globalisation for a lower-income country.
items.answer: Advantage: new jobs and investment from foreign companies, access to bigger export markets and technology. Disadvantage: low wages and poor conditions, profits sent abroad, local businesses unable to compete, loss of local culture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each with development [2]

items.stem: Approximate casualties (killed  wounded  missing and captured) in the Battle of the Somme  July-November 1916: British Empire 420 000  France 200 000  Germany 465 000. On the first day  1 July  the British suffered 57 470 casualties  of whom 19 240 were killed. Explain why casualties on the first day were so high.
items.answer: The week-long bombardment failed to destroy the barbed wire and deep German dugouts; troops walked slowly across no man’s land carrying heavy kit and were cut down by machine guns.
items.markingKey: 1 mark failed bombardment; 1 mark machine guns/tactics [2]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the natural process by which gases in the atmosphere trap heat radiated from the Earth’s surface, keeping the planet warm”.
items.answer: Greenhouse effect
items.markingKey: Greenhouse effect: the natural process by which gases in the atmosphere trap heat radiated from the Earth’s surface, keeping the planet warm. [1]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “self-rule or independence for India”.
items.answer: Swaraj
items.markingKey: Swaraj: self-rule or independence for India. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Most deaths in earthquakes are caused by collapsing buildings rather than the ground shaking itself.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Shaking rarely kills directly; collapsing buildings, fires, landslides and tsunamis cause most deaths.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Scenario: Police arrest a protester and keep him in prison for months without charge or trial. Which article of the UDHR is most clearly being broken?
options: Article 3: the right to life, liberty and security of person
Article 9: no one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile
Article 21: the right to take part in the government of one’s country, directly or through freely chosen representatives
Article 18: freedom of thought, conscience and religion
items.answer: Article 9: no one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile
items.markingKey: Article 9. [1]

items.stem: Explain why young adults are the group most likely to migrate to cities.
items.answer: They are looking for work and education, have fewer family responsibilities and are more willing to take risks; their move also increases cities’ birth rates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: Explain why canals were important in the early Industrial Revolution.
items.answer: They carried heavy, bulky goods such as coal cheaply and smoothly; the Bridgewater Canal (1761) roughly halved the price of coal in Manchester.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cheap bulk transport; 1 mark example/effect [2]

items.stem: On a 1:25 000 map, a footpath from the youth hostel to the windmill measures 4 cm. Calculate the real length of the footpath in kilometres. Show your working.
items.answer: 1 km

items.stem: Explain how consumers can influence the behaviour of TNCs.
items.answer: By choosing ethical or fair-trade brands, boycotting companies with poor records, using social media to expose problems and supporting campaigns, consumers can pressure TNCs to improve conditions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark how it creates pressure [2]

items.stem: A student investigating how attitudes to war were shown in memorials finds Source A. Source A: the inscription on a village war memorial in England, unveiled in 1921 (adapted). “To the glorious memory of the men of this parish who gave their lives for King and Country, 1914-1918. Their name liveth for evermore.” (a) What can you infer from Source A about how communities remembered the First World War in the 1920s? (b) Suggest the purpose of Source A. Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Communities in the 1920s remembered the dead as heroes who sacrificed themselves for a noble cause. (b) To honour the local dead and give families comfort and pride.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid inference; 1 mark supported with a detail from the source [2] (b) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: A school weather station recorded this data for one week. Maximum temperature (°C): Mon 18, Tue 12, Wed 17, Thu 16, Fri 16, Sat 18, Sun 15. Minimum temperature (°C): Mon 8, Tue 7, Wed 11, Thu 12, Fri 12, Sat 10, Sun 9. Rainfall (mm): Mon 15, Tue 12, Wed 12, Thu 0, Fri 15, Sat 6, Sun 1. Name the instrument used to measure each type of data in the table.
items.answer: Maximum-minimum (Six’s) thermometer for temperatures; rain gauge for rainfall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “African leaders were invited to the Berlin Conference of 1884-85.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. No Africans took part; Europeans divided the continent among themselves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A geographer scores two places at risk from earthquakes using the formula risk = hazard × vulnerability ÷ capacity to cope (all scores out of 10 except capacity, out of 4). Town C: hazard 9, vulnerability 6, capacity 2. City E: hazard 9, vulnerability 4, capacity 2. Suggest two ways to increase a place’s capacity to cope.
items.answer: Train emergency services, build earthquake-resistant hospitals, set up warning systems, hold drills, store emergency supplies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a pressure group and a political party.
items.answer: A political party stands candidates in elections and wants to form a government covering all issues; a pressure group tries to influence decisions on particular issues without standing for election.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each; 1 mark contrast [2]

items.stem: The table shows population and area for three regions of a country. River Delta: population 15 000 000  area 25 000 km². Highland Region: population 300 000  area 12 000 km². Northern District: population 2 250 000  area 25 000 km². (a) Suggest two reasons why Highland Region is sparsely populated. (b) Suggest two reasons why River Delta is densely populated.
items.answer: (a) Steep slopes, thin soils and a colder climate make farming and building difficult; poor transport. (b) Flat, fertile alluvial soil and water for farming (e.g. rice); river transport.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each reason [2] (b) 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: A student investigating why factory reform happened in the 1830s finds Source D. Source D: a letter by Richard Oastler, “Yorkshire Slavery”, published in the Leeds Mercury, 1830 (adapted). “Thousands of little children are this very moment existing in a state of slavery more horrid than the victims of colonial slavery, working from six in the morning to seven at night with only thirty minutes for food.” Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of the campaign for factory reform that Source D does not show.
items.answer: The views of mill owners, or what the law said at the time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark accurate own knowledge; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Two sources that agree must both be telling the truth.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They may share the same bias or one may have copied the other; agreement makes a claim stronger but does not prove it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: “Fair trade is the best way to reduce inequality between countries.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: scale of fair trade; investment and aid.
items.answer: Agree: Guaranteed minimum prices and premiums improve farmers’ incomes, schools and health care (e.g. Kenyan flower farms). Disagree: Fairtrade is a small share of world trade. Processing products locally, investment, education, debt relief and fairer trade rules may have bigger effects. Good governance and reducing conflict matter. Judgement: Fair trade helps specific communities but cannot on its own close the development gap.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Source A is taken from the diary of a Jewish teenager hiding in Amsterdam, 1943 (adapted). It says: “We hear that our Jewish friends are being taken away in groups. The Gestapo treat them roughly and transport them in cattle trucks to the camps in the east. We must keep very quiet here.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) Suggest the purpose of Source A. Explain your answer. (b) Explain one reason why Source A may be reliable and one reason why it may not be reliable.
items.answer: (a) To record private thoughts and experiences during hiding. (b) May be reliable: it is a personal account written at the time by someone directly affected. May not be reliable: the writer heard about deportations second-hand and could only know part of what was happening.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2] (b) 2 marks for each explained reason based on provenance (author, date, purpose) [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that mitigation is more important than adaptation in responding to climate change. You may wish to consider: poorer countries; sea defences.
items.answer: Agree: Cutting emissions tackles the cause; without mitigation warming will continue and adaptation will become impossible in some places. Disagree: Some climate change is already happening, so adaptation is needed now to protect lives (sea walls, flood warnings, drought-resistant crops). Poorer countries contributing few emissions need adaptation most. Judgement: Both are essential: mitigation limits future change while adaptation protects people from changes already happening.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: “The economic impact was the most important effect of colonial rule on colonised peoples.” How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. You may wish to consider: culture and education; land and labour.
items.answer: Agree: Land was taken, taxes forced wage labour and economies were based on exporting cash crops and minerals. Local industries declined and wealth flowed to Europe. Disagree: Cultural effects – language, religion, education – were deep and long-lasting. Political effects such as new borders and loss of self-rule shaped later conflicts. Violence and loss of life, e.g. in the Congo, were devastating. Judgement: Economic effects were central to why empires existed, but cultural and political effects lasted longest.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: Scientists measure that the Pacific plate sliding past the North American plate along the San Andreas Fault move past each other at about 4 cm per year. (a) Calculate how far they move in 100 000 years  in kilometres. (b) Explain what causes the plates to move.
items.answer: (a) 4 km (b) Convection currents in the mantle, together with ridge push and slab pull.

items.stem: How far do you agree that informal settlements should be cleared and replaced with new apartment blocks? Use your own knowledge to support your answer. You may wish to consider: communities and jobs; upgrading schemes.
items.answer: Agree: New blocks could provide safe buildings, water and sanitation. Land could be used more efficiently. Disagree: Clearance destroys communities, informal businesses and livelihoods (e.g. Dharavi’s recycling industry). New flats may be unaffordable or far from jobs. Upgrading schemes such as Rio’s Favela Bairro improved conditions while keeping communities. Judgement: Upgrading with residents’ involvement is usually better than clearance, though some unsafe areas may need rehousing.
items.markingKey: Level 1: simple, generalised statements. Level 2: explains one side with accurate supporting detail. Level 3: explains both sides with detail. Level 4 (top marks): balanced, well-supported argument and a reasoned judgement on "how far".

items.stem: A student tested the hypothesis “Traffic is heavier near the town centre than on the edge of town.” Counts of vehicles in one hour: near the centre 158, on the edge of town 68. Data was collected once, on a weekday morning. (a) Does the evidence support the hypothesis? Use figures in your answer. (b) Identify one limitation of the data and explain how it affects the conclusion. (c) Suggest two improvements to make the conclusion more reliable.
items.answer: (a) Supported: the centre had 158 vehicles and the edge 68, a difference of 90 (132.4% of the lower value). (b) Data collected only once/at one place and time (e.g. one weekday morning or at the park entrance on a Sunday), so it may not be representative and the conclusion is tentative. (c) Repeat on different days and times; increase the sample/sites; use systematic sampling; compare with secondary data.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark figures [2] (b) 1 mark limitation; 1 mark effect [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Source B is taken from a German newspaper editorial, July 1914 (adapted). It says: “Serbia has shed royal blood and must be punished. If Russia stands behind Serbia, Germany will stand beside Austria-Hungary as a loyal ally. We are surrounded by enemies who envy our strength.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) Suggest the purpose of Source B. Explain your answer. (b) Explain one reason why Source B may be reliable and one reason why it may not be reliable.
items.answer: (a) To persuade German readers to support the government’s backing of Austria-Hungary. (b) May be reliable: it shows views published in Germany during the crisis. May not be reliable: a single newspaper may reflect government influence and nationalist feeling rather than all opinion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2] (b) 2 marks for each explained reason based on provenance (author, date, purpose) [4]
